reviews.critic: Adversarial review of the two "adaptation" ideas (economics and competition; evidence and testability). Overall: neither idea is a market edge, and both designers say so. Their arithmetic is honest and I reproduced it on in-sample trades. The League is worth building only in a stripped form, as the forward-test harness that every later idea needs; its nightly AI rule generator is the weak part. Three clocks is a short checklist (measure crypto costs at signal time, fix a bet size) wrapped in an untestable gate, and should be folded into the League's first stage. One constraint hits both: every fractional risk step (quarter unit, half risk, 0.5 % per trade) needs an account of roughly 2,500 to 11,000 EUR because the minimum lot already risks 10 to 14 USD per trade. Neither gives the user new trades or daily adaptation within two years.

reviews.name: The League: permanent paper twins, real money only on evidence dated after the freeze, supplied by a rate-limited AI research loop
reviews.fatal_flaw:
The forward-dated core holds, but the part that is supposed to add trades (the nightly AI generator and its probation gate) breaks at five points.

1. The output rate equals the false-positive rate. Two families a week of 60 configurations is about 6,200 new trials a year. At the in-sample bar of t >= 3.0 (one-sided p = 0.00135), pure noise supplies about 8 admissions a year. A zero-edge rule passes the validation criteria (PF >= 1.06, 3 of 4 years) roughly 15-20 % of the time on my rough estimate. That gives 1-2 probation seats a year from noise alone, which is exactly the "few probation seats a year" promised.

2. The probation gate still uses the 2022-2025 validation look, and that look is not out of sample for a rule written by a language model. The model knows gold and bitcoin trended in 2022-2025, and the validation log already has 397 access lines. The group gate is also soft: "pooled paper record positive over 3,000 trades" passes about 31 % of the time for a generator that only pays costs (standard error 0.04 R with design effect 2.5).

3. Paper fills are not validated for paper seats.
- The parity test compares one simulation with another, with a tolerance (median 0.05 R) as large as the whole expected edge of an admitted rule (+0.02 to +0.05 R).
- The dead-rule control fires only above +0.03 R after 2,000 trades. It misses a fill bias of 0.03 R about 70 % of the time.
- It needs 1-1.5 years to accumulate, after the first probations.
- "MT5 one-minute bid/ask history" does not exist: a bar carries bid prices plus one spread value, minimum or maximum depending on the build.

4. A "quarter unit" is not implementable at small size. Minimum-lot risk is 10-14 USD per trade on us100, gold and bitcoin (lab figures). A quarter of 0.5 % needs an account of about 8,000-11,000 EUR.

5. The only conclusive test takes 18-24 months at 25-31 % power for the designer's own expected value. API cost is probably 2-4 times the estimate, because agentic research sessions are not 1-2 cent calls.

Stage 0 can hardly fail: the families were chosen knowing 2019-2021, and 2020 flatters every breakout rule.
reviews.strongest_point: It is the only design in which the language model's memory leak, the 1,500-trial selection problem and faster competitors are all irrelevant by construction, because only records dated after a code freeze count. The speed-limit arithmetic is correct and I reproduced it. It also turns the lab's dead rules into negative controls. Stage 1 (twins, controls, coin-flip twins, no P&L conclusion at 60 days) is cheap, quick and needed by every other idea, including any model-as-trader test after the knowledge cut-off.
reviews.better_variant:
Build the harness and drop the nightly generator.

1. Make the primary pre-registered test the forward record of the frozen eleven-sleeve portfolio: an anytime-valid meter with a threshold of 20, expected in about 2.5 years at validation level.
2. Replace pure paper with micro-live sampling: 0.01-lot real fills on a random 10-20 % of gold, FX and crypto bench trades (cents per trade). Estimate the signed fill bias with a confidence interval, not a median absolute difference.
3. Log ticks from the live terminal through the existing bridge; do not replay one-minute bars.
4. Run the false-discovery control over 4-5 mechanism families, not 30 seats. The first promotion then needs a meter of 25, not 150.
5. Take no validation look for AI-written rules. Probation comes only from a forward paper record: a seat meter of at least 5 plus a positive family pool.
6. Limit generation to one family a month, replications of published rules with a stated mechanism only.
7. Spend the API budget on forward-only contestants (news, a daily risk dial), where the leak cannot occur.
8. State the account size at which fractional seats exist.

reviews.name: Three clocks: a risk engine that learns costs in weeks and edges in years, and refuses every faster adaptation (a discipline, not an edge)
reviews.fatal_flaw:
There is no edge to show and no experiment that can fail.

1. The gate is unfalsifiable. Its own stated effect is -0.005 to +0.01 R per trade. With a trade standard deviation of 1.4 R and design effect 2.5, confirming +0.01 R needs about 196,000 trades, roughly 145 years.

2. The first experiment keeps the gate whatever happens ("useful" or "silent alarm"). Its "useful" criterion, a deviation above 25 % on at least one of eleven sleeves, will fire from noise: about 8 signals per sleeve in four weeks, and about 25 real fills against slippage noise of several basis points.

3. The gate ratio is false precision. Its numerator is a validation expectancy whose standard error is as large as itself.
- brk72 bitcoin: +0.041 R at t 0.77, standard error 0.053 R.
- nq_btc_follow: +0.049 R at t 1.73, so the ratio is 3.4 with a one-sigma range of 2.0 to 4.9.
A 25 % cost change moves the ratio less than that noise. On/half/off is decided by a frozen noisy number, not by the measured cost.

4. The only material unknown, the ether spread (1.16 to 4.32 USD), is already item 2 of the to-do list in COSTS_FP.md. It is a reading in MT5, not an idea.

5. It breaks its own rule against reacting to noise. "Negative calendar year: risk halved" fires 22 % of years at the designer's own prior (half of validation) against 50 % with no edge. That is 2.3 to 1, the ratio the same designer calls "not evidence" elsewhere. The +/- 25 % yearly cap contradicts the formula's 0.50 % to 0.16 % and the halving.

6. It asks for two more validation looks, and tunes the ladder on validation trades. The weights test is a coin flip: an expected gain of +0.03 Sharpe against a four-year standard error of 0.2-0.3.

7. Half risk and 0.5 % sizing do not exist at minimum lot (10-14 USD risk per trade) below an account of about 2,500-3,000 EUR.

The "in-sample checks" that reject bandits, winner-chasing and volatility sizing are not in any trial log I found.
reviews.strongest_point:
Two observations are worth keeping.

1. A real hole in the lab's cost model. The frames apply a clipped Dukascopy spread shape, while the sleeves enter on volatility bursts (a 6-sigma Nasdaq minute, 09:34, breakout closes). Crypto is 59 % of trades and sits only 2.5-3.6 times above modelled cost. Measuring the spread at signal time is free and takes weeks.

2. The bet-size table is the most decision-relevant number for a user who only cares about percentages. It reproduces: Sharpe 1.56 at validation level and 0.78 at half, a negative year 6 % / 22 % / 50 % of the time. 2 % per trade is over-betting if the truth is half of validation.
reviews.better_variant:
Fold it into Stage 1 of the League as a cost logger with one pre-registered rule and no validation re-look.

1. Log every tick for two minutes either side of each signal, pooled per instrument, not per sleeve.
2. Take 0.01-lot real fills for signed slippage over three months, not four weeks.
3. Use the stress test the lab already ran: every sleeve passed PF >= 1.04 at costs x 1.5. If the measured round-trip cost at signal time exceeds 1.5 times the model, the sleeve is outside its tested envelope and goes to paper until re-validated. Otherwise nothing changes.
4. Fix the bet size once: 0.25-0.5 % per trade, or minimum lot if larger, with the account size stated.
5. Keep a single drawdown rule: -90 R from the peak or a negative two-year total means paper only (1.7 % against 29 %, and 1 % against 51 %, are real evidence). Drop the calendar-year halving.
6. Record the rejected adaptive schemes as logged trials or not at all.

ideas.name: Gamma gate: run the us100 noise-area momentum sleeve at full size only when dealer option gamma is low
ideas.pitch: Each morning the robot reads one public number, the previous day's estimate of option dealers' gamma on the S&P 500, and ranks it against the past year. On low-gamma days it runs the validated us100 momentum sleeve at double risk, and on the other days at half risk or not at all.
ideas.mechanism:
Who pays: option dealers who are short gamma must buy as the index rises and sell as it falls, to stay hedged. That forced, price-insensitive trading creates intraday trend. When dealers are long gamma they do the opposite and damp moves. Baltussen, Da, Lammers and Martens (JFE 2021) find intraday momentum on the S&P only when net gamma is negative.

Why it persists: the hedging is mechanical risk control, not a view, and the option buyers on the other side pay for it knowingly. Faster players cannot remove it because the flow lasts hours and scales with the move itself.

What I measured in-sample (2014-2021, frozen noise30 rule, the lab's cost frames, gamma series from the free SqueezeMetrics file, previous day's value ranked against the prior 252 days):
- us100, lowest third of gamma: 591 trades, +0.173 R, PF 1.63, +8.2 bp net per trade.
- us100, other two thirds: 1,052 trades, +0.031 R, PF 1.11, +1.7 bp net.
- Difference z = 2.6; positive in all 9 window / threshold variants (z 1.5 to 2.6); low beats rest in 6 of 8 years, but not in 2014 or 2021.
- Day level: 47.8 % winning days in the low third against 39.9 %.
- It is not a volatility effect: the same split on trailing 20-day realised volatility shows no gradient (+0.071 R against +0.081 R).
- us500 goes the same way but weaker (low third +0.094 R, PF 1.30, t 2.2; rest +0.014 R); us30 has the same sign and no tradable edge.
- The opening-candle sleeve ocm4 shows no such gradient (+0.066 R low against +0.165 R rest), so the gate must not be applied to it.
ideas.role_of_ai:
None in the trade decision; a plain algorithm does all of it. It downloads the gamma file before 09:30 New York, computes the percentile and writes a regime flag that the MT5 robot reads.

The language model has two support jobs, about 30 calls a month:
- A nightly check that the gamma file updated and is plausible, with a second estimate computed from the free delayed CBOE option chain as cross-check and fallback.
- A monthly written review of whether the low-gamma and other days still differ.

This is a regime variable that changes day by day, not a model that learns; the user should be told so.
ideas.instruments: us100 CFD (existing noise30 sleeve). Optional second sleeve, judged separately: the same rule on us500, low-gamma days only.
ideas.trades_per_day: No new trades on us100: the sleeve keeps about 0.8 trade per session and only the risk per trade changes. The optional us500 sleeve would add about 0.3 trade a day (80 a year), highly correlated with us100.
ideas.holding_time: Unchanged: 30 minutes to 6 hours, flat by 15:55 New York.
ideas.edge_vs_cost:
Round-trip cost on us100 is about 0.8 bp. In-sample net per trade: +8.2 bp in the low-gamma third against +1.7 bp otherwise, so the gate moves risk from trades earning about twice their cost to trades earning about ten times it.

In-sample, the low third made 100 R of the sleeve's 127 R with 36 % of the trades. Doubling risk there and halving it elsewhere, at about the same average risk, would have given about 214 R, 68 % more. That figure is overstated by selection; if the effect is real I would expect 20-30 % more profit for the same risk and a few points more winning days.
ideas.data_needed:
- SqueezeMetrics DIX.csv: free, daily since May 2011, updated every evening. It is a single third-party file, which is a dependency risk.
- Fallback: the free delayed CBOE option chain for SPX (open interest and gamma per strike). It has no history, so it can only be checked forward.
- The lab's us100 and us500 frames and its saved noise30 trades.

The file measures open interest and misses same-day options, which have been about half of S&P option volume since 2022. That is the main reason the effect may have changed.
ideas.first_experiment:
Step 1, half a day, no API cost. The lead joins the frozen gate (previous day's gamma below the 33rd percentile of the prior 252 days) to the noise30 validation trades of 2022-2025, about 730 trades of which about 240 fall in the low third. This is one logged look at validation.

Pass rule fixed now, all three required:
- low-third expectancy minus the rest is at least +0.10 R;
- low-third PF is at least 1.25;
- low beats rest in at least 3 of the 4 years.

If there is no real effect this passes about 7 % of the time; if the in-sample gap of 0.14 R is real it passes about 55 % of the time.

Step 2, only after a pass: 60 sessions on demo computing gamma from the CBOE chain alongside the file; the two percentile series must correlate above 0.8.

The us500 sleeve gets its own single look: low-gamma trades PF at least 1.12 and positive in 3 of 4 years.

My in-sample scripts are /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-gold-orb/340d9f5a-4d28-5733-90cb-10a10699d00b/scratchpad/code/an2.py and /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-gold-orb/340d9f5a-4d28-5733-90cb-10a10699d00b/scratchpad/code/an4.py.
ideas.kill_rule:
- Any of the three validation conditions fails: drop the gate and keep the sleeve at equal risk. No second threshold, window or gamma source may be tried on validation.
- Live: if after 150 gated trades the low-gamma trades do not earn more per trade than the others, switch the gate off.
- If the file stops updating and the CBOE estimate has not passed the 0.8 correlation check, switch the gate off.
ideas.differs_from_failed:
- It predicts no direction and adds no entry rule; it sizes a sleeve that already passed validation.
- The conditioning variable comes from option positioning, not price. The lab's price-feature models found nothing on us100, and trailing volatility does not reproduce the split.
- End-of-day momentum failed in the lab unconditionally, and my check shows that conditioning on the size of the day's move (the leveraged-ETF story) fails too. Gamma is the one conditioning that separates the days in-sample.

ideas.name: Fixing-flow calendar: buy back the dollar right after the month-end London fix, in the direction hedgers were forced to trade (plus a Tokyo settlement-day leg judged separately)
ideas.pitch: On the last weekday of each month, funds that hedge their US shares must trade dollars at the 16:00 London benchmark, and the direction is known in advance from how the S&P 500 did that month. The robot takes the other side at 16:00 for 30 minutes on six or seven dollar pairs, when the pressure lifts and the price comes back.
ideas.mechanism:
Who pays: foreign funds holding US shares with a currency hedge. When US shares rose over the month they are under-hedged and must sell dollars at the month-end WM/R fix; when shares fell they must buy. They are measured against the fix rate, so they do not care about the impact they cause (Melvin and Prins, 2015). Banks execute these orders inside the five-minute fix window, the price is pushed, and it reverts once the window closes.

Why it persists: the flow is an obligation on a fixed date, and since the fix scandal banks carry less of their own risk around the window. Faster players take part of it: in my data the reversal happens between 16:02 and 16:10, entry at 16:05 keeps half and entry at 16:10 nothing. A robot firing at 16:00-16:02 is fast enough.

In-sample, 2013-2021, 108 month-ends, 7 dollar pairs, the lab's bid / ask frames. Rule: at 16:00 London buy dollars if the S&P 500 is up on the month as of the previous close, sell if down, exit 16:30.
- Gross +4.7 bp, net +3.75 bp per trade; t = 4.8 computed on the 108 dates; 73 % of dates positive.
- The sign matters: in up months the dollar rises after the fix (+4.3 bp net, t 5.3, 81 dates); in down months it falls (-3.9 bp for a dollar buyer, t -2.0, 27 dates).
- Dose-response: month-to-date move under 2 %: -0.15 bp; 2-4 %: +6.7 bp (91 % of 33 dates positive); over 4 %: +6.9 bp (89 % of 28 dates).
- Placebos: the same trade 1, 2, 3, 5 or 10 days before month-end gives -1.6 to -0.1 bp net; 17:00-18:00 on month-end gives -0.6 bp.
- By period: +2.3 bp (2013-15), +2.7 bp (2016-18), +6.3 bp (2019-21).
- Six of seven pairs are positive (t 1.9 to 5.6); the yen is flat.

Tokyo leg, weaker. On settlement days (the 5th, 10th, 15th, 20th, 25th and month-end, 676 days) Japanese importers buy dollars at the 09:55 Tokyo fix. Long usdjpy 09:30 to 09:55, then short 09:55 to 10:30: +2.0 bp net per day for the pair of trades, t 3.8, 7 of 9 years positive. On other days both legs lose after costs. The effect sits on one minute: an entry one minute late halves it.
ideas.role_of_ai:
None in the trade decision. A plain algorithm computes the S&P 500 month-to-date sign from the previous close, knows the calendar and sends the orders at 16:00:00 London and 09:30 / 09:55 Tokyo.

Language-model jobs, a few calls a month:
- Keep the calendar right: UK, US and Japanese holidays move the month-end fix and the settlement days. My test ignored Japanese holidays.
- Optional and forward-only: read the public summaries of the banks' month-end rebalancing models and extract the consensus direction as a second opinion. That gives 12 readings a year, so it can never be proven and is logged only, not traded.
ideas.instruments: Month-end leg: eurusd, gbpusd, audusd, nzdusd, usdcad, usdchf (usdjpy optional; flat in-sample). Tokyo leg: usdjpy only.
ideas.trades_per_day: Month-end leg: 6-7 trades on 12 days a year, effectively one dollar bet a month. Tokyo leg: 2 trades on about 75 days a year. Together about 0.9 trade per trading day on average, bunched on calendar days. This does not deliver several trades every day.
ideas.holding_time: 30 minutes for the month-end leg; 25 and 35 minutes for the two Tokyo trades.
ideas.edge_vs_cost:
Month-end leg: gross +4.7 bp against about 1 bp round-trip cost on the basket (0.6-1.7 bp by pair, already in the frames), so about 4.7 times cost. It survives a tripling of cost at about +1.7 bp.

Per month-end the basket earned +3.75 bp net with a standard deviation of about 8 bp across dates. At 2 % total risk spread over six pairs that is about +0.5 % of the account per month-end in-sample, roughly 6 % a year; plan on half.

Tokyo leg: gross about 1.6 and 2.0 bp per trade against about 0.75 bp cost, so 2.1 to 2.6 times cost; net +0.8 and +1.2 bp. That is thin and sits at the lab's own fragility line.
ideas.data_needed: All already in the lab: one-minute bid / ask frames for the seven dollar pairs (2013 onward) and S&P 500 daily closes (any free source; I took them from the SqueezeMetrics file). Nothing else. Validation needs 2022-2025 of the same frames: 48 month-ends and about 300 settlement days.
ideas.kill_rule:
- Each leg lives or dies alone on its single validation look; no re-signing, no new window, no filter added afterwards.
- Live: kill a leg if the measured FP spread at the entry minute is more than twice the frame's.
- Month-end leg: kill after 12 live month-ends with a negative basket sum.
- Tokyo leg: kill after 100 live settlement days with a negative net sum.
ideas.differs_from_failed:
- The lab's currency track tested a cousin (B1: at the month-end fix, fade the previous hour's move): +0.85 bp net, t 1.3, failed. This rule takes its sign from the hedgers' obligation, a public number known the day before. The two disagree on 44 % of pair-dates, and on those this rule still earns +2.1 bp net (t 2.3).
- It is not a night or calendar window collecting market beta: the sign flips with the S&P's month, and the same clock on other days gives nothing.
- It is a fade in form, but of a flow whose direction and time are known beforehand, not of a price pattern.
- Weak points an auditor should press: I looked at six windows before settling on this one; 108 dates is a small sample; the 2 % dose-response buckets were chosen by me; the Tokyo leg depends on a single minute.

dropped_by_designer: Leveraged-ETF rebalancing at the close (trade 15:30-15:55 New York in the direction of the day's move when it exceeds 1 %): in-sample +1.25 bp on us100 (t 0.7, 568 days) and -1.0 bp on us500, no dose-response with the size of the move. Dead.

Crypto funding rate as a crowding filter on the validated hourly breakouts (Binance funding history, 2020-2021, about 300 trades per coin): on bitcoin, breakouts with the crowd did better (+0.26 R against +0.11 R); on ether the opposite (+0.06 R against +0.43 R). Contradictory, so noise.

Crypto open interest (rising or falling, high or low level) as a breakout filter: bitcoin, September 2020 to 2021, 207 trades, no separation (+0.14 R when rising over 24 hours, +0.17 R when falling). Free ether history before December 2021 is missing.

Fading bitcoin liquidation cascades: no free liquidation history before 2022 (Binance files return 404 for 2020-21), so forward-only at about one event a day against 4 bp cost, with the first seconds of the rebound taken by faster players. I put it at 10 % or less.
Trading around perpetual funding stamps (00 / 08 / 16 UTC): the price effect is capped by the funding payment itself (1-10 bp) against 4 bp cost.
Spot bitcoin ETF creations at the 15:00-16:00 New York benchmark window: data only since 2024 (inside validation and holdout), and in-kind creations since mid-2025 removed most of the forced window.

Trading into the month-end fix (the original Melvin-Prins leg, 15:00-16:00 London): in-sample +2.7 bp gross (t 1.55), decaying from +7.9 bp in 2013-14 to -1.3 bp in 2019-21. Only the post-fix leg is kept.
Daily London fix reversal on all days: real before costs (0.6-1.3 bp gross, t 3 to 5 on each of 7 pairs) but below the 0.85-2 bp cost. The lab's currency track reached the same conclusion.
Gamma gate on the opening-candle sleeve ocm4: no gradient (+0.066 R on low-gamma days against +0.165 R on the rest). Opening momentum is not a hedging effect.
Fading moves on high-gamma days: momentum there is zero, not negative (-0.75 bp, 49 % winners), so nothing is left to fade after costs.

Option-expiry pinning and same-day option gamma estimated from the delayed CBOE chain: no free history, the sign of customer flow is unknown, and forward-only at 1-2 trades a day gives too little power.

Currency option expiries at the 10:00 New York cut (public daily lists a language model could parse): currencies have the worst cost-to-move ratio (about 12 % of an hourly move), the expected pin is a few bp, and there is no clean history. I put it at 5 % or less.
Gold futures positioning (weekly CFTC report) as a filter for the gold sleeves: weekly data gives too few independent observations for an intraday rule, and it is widely used already.
Quarter-end pension rebalancing on index CFDs: 4-12 events a year, and the lab's calendar-window work already found only market beta there.

reviews.name: Gamma gate: run the us100 noise-area momentum sleeve at full size only when dealer option gamma is low
reviews.fatal_flaw:
The split is real in-sample but it is not a gamma effect, and the proposed sizing costs more than it is likely to earn.

1. A price-only variable reproduces it. I reproduced the designer's split (+0.169 R on 591 trades against +0.026 R on 1,052, z 2.66). The same split on the S&P 500's trailing 5-day return (lowest third of the past year) gives +0.161 R against +0.021 R, z 2.65. The two variables correlate 0.57. With the 20-day drawdown in a regression, gamma's coefficient is 0.01 (t 0.09). The designer tested only 20-day realised volatility, so "it comes from option positioning, not price" is not supported. Caveat: I tried six lookbacks (z from -0.4 to 2.65), so my proxy is selected too.

2. The mechanism's fingerprints are missing. The effect is reversed on the other us100 momentum sleeve (ocm4), weaker on us500, where the gamma is actually measured, and absent on us30. It reverses in 2021, the last in-sample year.

3. The statistics are thin. z 2.6 is the best of 9 variants across 3 instruments and 2 sleeves. The linear day-clustered t is -1.7. Ten of 410 low-gamma days supply 52 of the 100 R.

4. The headline numbers flatter it.
- "8.2 bp against 1.7 bp" is partly scale: stops are 73 bp on low-gamma days against 50 bp.
- "68 % more profit" is +23 % in risk-adjusted terms (daily mean / sd 0.114 against 0.093).
- If there is no effect, 2x / 0.5x sizing loses 18 % of risk-adjusted return, and the worst day goes from -2.3 R to -4.6 R.

5. The tests are weak.
- Validation: the sleeve itself is at t 1.89 there (850 trades, +0.055 R; the designer assumed about 730). A pass at 7 % false-positive and about 55 % power is a likelihood ratio of about 8, on a second look at a marginal sleeve.
- Live kill rule: after 150 trades the standard error of the difference is about 0.2 R against a claimed effect of 0.14 R, so it cannot decide anything.

6. The gamma file counts open interest and misses same-day options, which is exactly what changed from 2022.

It adds no trades and no winning days, and the two language-model jobs are a file-freshness check a short script does.
reviews.strongest_point: Costs do not matter here (no new trades) and latency is irrelevant. The direction agrees with published work: Baltussen, Da, Lammers and Martens (JFE 2021) find index intraday momentum only when net gamma is negative. A circular-shift permutation of the gamma series gives p = 0.0025 for the tercile gap, and a 60-day-lagged gamma shows nothing (+0.075 R against +0.078 R), so some real "stressed market" regime dependence of this sleeve is likely. In-sample, the 840 trades where neither gamma nor the 5-day return is low earn exactly 0.000 R. The pass rule is fixed in advance and takes half a day.
reviews.better_variant:
Treat it as a "stressed-market" gate, not a gamma gate.
- Freeze two flags before the validation look: gamma in the lowest third, and the S&P 5-day return in the lowest third.
- Pre-declare that the price-only flag is adopted if it does as well, which removes the third-party file and the same-day-option blind spot.
- Use 1.5x / 0.75x weights: under no effect that costs 6 % of risk-adjusted return, not 18 %; in-sample it keeps most of the gain (daily t 3.75 against 3.91).

reviews.name: Fixing-flow calendar: buy back the dollar right after the month-end London fix, in the direction hedgers were forced to trade (plus a Tokyo settlement-day leg judged separately)
reviews.fatal_flaw:
The month-end leg survives; the Tokyo leg does not. No single flaw kills the month-end leg, but these weaken it.

Month-end leg
1. Half the rule is unproven. "Sell dollars in down months" rests on 7 dates in 2019-2021 (+12.7 bp, including February and March 2020). On the 19 down months of 2013-2018 it earned -0.26 bp. Validation has many more down months, so the basket will be diluted if only the up-month half is real.
2. The edge sits in a three-minute band. Entry 16:00 to 16:02 nets +3.7 to +4.0 bp, 16:03 +2.9, 16:05 +2.1, 16:07 +0.9. This is the most watched minute of the FX month; if the reversal has moved two minutes earlier since 2021, a retail entry gets half.
3. The story is not quite what the data shows. The visible push into the fix is only 1 to 2 bp over the last 30 minutes (t 1 to 2), against +4.9 bp afterwards. Fading the actual basket move into the fix earns nothing (t under 1). Only the S&P sign carries the information.
4. The frame may understate the spread. It shows no widening at the month-end fix (median 0.82 bp against 0.85 on other days).
5. The yen was dropped after seeing it flat, which lifts the in-sample mean from 3.75 to 4.5 bp.
6. It is 12 independent bets a year: about +0.5 % per month-end in-sample at 2 % risk, so plan on about 3 % a year. It does nothing for "several trades a day" and uses no AI.
7. The live kill rule is slow. A negative sum after 12 month-ends happens 50 % of the time with no edge and about 21 % with half the edge.
8. Trade press (FullFX, 2023) reports funds now deliver month-end orders in the days before, with a smaller fix impact.

Tokyo leg: weak to dead
- Both trades use the same single 09:55:00 quote. One minute off, the long nets +0.17 bp and the short +0.60 bp, about 0.8 bp for the pair against 1.5 bp of cost.
- 2014 and 2015 are negative; 2018 and 2021 are under 1 bp.
- It is the best-known retail pattern in Japan, so fills at that second will be worse than the frame.
reviews.strongest_point:
The in-sample evidence is the strongest of the two ideas and I could not break it.
- Reproduced exactly: +3.75 bp net on 108 dates, t 4.8, 73 % of dates positive.
- Every year 2013-2021 is positive (+1.0 to +9.4 bp on six pairs).
- Without the five best dates it is still +3.4 bp, t 4.6.
- The dollar's own month-to-date move does not reproduce it (fading it: t 0.6), and the rule still earns +2.9 bp (t 2.8) on the 46 dates where the two signs disagree.
- Placebo days and hours are flat or negative.
- Gross is about 4.7 times cost and survives a tripling.
- Latency does not matter: entry at 16:01 or 16:02 is as good as 16:00.

The mechanism is documented independently (Melvin and Prins 2015; Evans 2018 finds larger post-fix reversals at month-end). The validation sample exists, is free and has 48 dates. The pass rule is fixed and passes under 3 % of the time by chance. No language model is involved, so there is no memory leak.
reviews.better_variant:
Month-end leg
- Freeze entry at 16:02 London, just before the window closes at 16:02:30, not at 16:00:00. In-sample it is the same (+3.99 bp against +3.91), and it avoids buying mid-window, where real retail spread and slippage are worst.
- Pre-declare a separate read-out for up months and down months (reported, not used for the pass), so a validation pass says whether to run the down-month half.
- Size each date by the capped size of the S&P's monthly move, as a declared secondary hypothesis, not a filter.
- Log the real FP Markets spread at 16:00-16:03 on the next month-ends now, before the validation look.
- Live rule: 24 month-ends, or stop at a -4 % drawdown on the leg.

Tokyo leg
- Drop it, or keep only the short entered at 09:56 and exited at 10:30.
- Require a pass with costs multiplied by 1.5.

ideas.name: Third clock: Tokyo-session index momentum on JP225 (HK50 and AUS200 only if their measured cost is under 2 bp)
ideas.pitch: Run the two index rules that already passed on us100 (noise-area momentum and the opening-candle rule), with parameters frozen, on the Japanese index during its own cash session, while the US book is asleep. It is the only place in the broker's list where I found both a mechanism and bets that are truly independent of the existing ones.
ideas.mechanism: Other side: intraday liquidity providers and mean-reversion traders who absorb forced, price-insensitive flow. Daily rebalancing of leveraged and inverse Nikkei ETFs and dealers hedging retail options and structured products (callable bull/bear contracts in Hong Kong) must buy after a rise and sell after a fall on the same day; the same mechanism as the lab's us100 sleeves. They keep losing on the minority of days when the flow is large, because the flow is mandated. It persists because 2-4 bp per trade is too small for a fund after market impact. Speed does not help: the push builds over hours, so faster players are part of the trend, not competitors for it. Evidence from my in-sample replica: the effect is equity-specific (12/12 index cells positive, FX negative), and results of Asian-hours trades are uncorrelated with US-session trades (0.00 to -0.04; Europe vs US +0.27). Counter-evidence: US index CFDs traded in Asian hours earn only +1.3 to +1.6 bp gross (net +0.1 to +0.6), so the home index is needed; the DAX in its home session earns +1.2 bp gross (t 1.05, net -0.1), so Europe is excluded; strength per trade varies from 0.02 standard deviation (us30, ger40) to 0.08 (us100), and us100 looks special.
ideas.role_of_ai: None in the trading decision: a plain algorithm computes the band and sends the orders. The lab's three blind tests say a language model adds no direction, and nothing in this lens changes that. The only adaptive piece is a nightly plain-statistics monitor that re-estimates each sleeve's real cost and edge with shrinkage and switches a sleeve off; a language model may write the evening phone note (one call a day, under 1 USD a month). That falls short of 'AI at 100 %' and I am saying so.
ideas.instruments: JP225 first. HK50 and AUS200 only if the spread read in the user's MT5 gives a round trip under 2 bp (other brokers show 9-21 points on HK50, about 3.5-8 bp, which would kill it; AUS200 1-3 points, about 1.1-3.4 bp against a small expected edge).
ideas.holding_time: 30 minutes to 6 hours, always flat before the Tokyo cash close; no overnight position.
ideas.trades_per_day: About 1.3 a day on JP225 (0.8 noise-area + 0.5 opening-candle), up to about 3 if HK50 and AUS200 qualify. Effective independent bets added: about 1 (1.5 with all three). Share of winning days: essentially unchanged, 45 % to roughly 46 %; winning months up by 1-2 points if the sleeve is as good as the us500 version. Its value is an extra uncorrelated bet and a faster verdict on the family, not more green days.
ideas.edge_vs_cost: Trade standard deviation on JP225 in the Tokyo session about 40-45 bp (assumed: half of an 80-85 bp session move). Gross = strength x 42 bp: 0.9 bp if us30-like, 2.3 bp if us500-like, 3.5 bp if us100-like. Cost: FP's JP225 spread is unknown; other brokers quote 6-16 points at an index near 50,000 = 1.2-3.2 bp, plus 0.4 bp slippage = 1.6-3.6 bp round trip. Net ranges from -2.7 to +1.9 bp, central case about zero. A pass needs both us100-like strength and a spread of 7 points or less.
ideas.first_experiment: Step 0 (10 minutes, free): read in MT5 the live spread of JP225, HK50, AUS200 during one cash session each, plus minimum lot and step. Step 1 (1.5-2 days, no API cost): download Dukascopy JPN.IDX/JPY one-minute bid/ask for 2013-2021 only, build the FP-cost frame, run noise30 and ocm4 with nothing changed except the clock (09:00 open, 15:00 close, no checks in the 11:30-12:30 lunch break). 2 configurations per index, all logged. Sample: about 1,550 noise-area and 950 opening-candle trades in-sample. Pass rule fixed now (lab criteria): net PF >= 1.12, t >= 2.5, at least 60 % of years positive, PF >= 1.04 with costs x1.5, random-entry null >= 97.5th percentile, long and short both positive. Only then the single validation run on 2022-2025, then demo. Power: us100-like strength gives an expected t of 3.2; us500-like gives 2.1 and fails, which is the correct outcome at these costs.
ideas.kill_rule: Stop at the first of: JP225 round trip above 2.0 bp in MT5; in-sample gross PF below 1.15 or net t below 2.5; validation fails; on demo, measured cost per trade above 1.5x the modelled cost over the first 50 trades.
ideas.differs_from_failed: Not an opening-range breakout (failed on indices, DAX, gold), not a calendar or night window (direction comes from the day's own move, long and short), not lead-lag between indices. It is a frozen transfer of the two rules that passed on us100 to a time zone the lab has never tested; the FX transfers that failed used the gold and crypto rules, and my check shows why FX cannot work (it mean-reverts intraday).
ideas.data_needed: Dukascopy JPN.IDX/JPY (and HKG.IDX/HKD, AUS.IDX/AUD if step 0 allows), one-minute bid and ask, free, 2013-2021 for the in-sample run and 2022-2025 kept untouched for the single validation. Live spreads and contract size from the user's own MT5.

ideas.name: Small-cap leg: US2000 with the two frozen us100 rules, judged on what it adds beyond us100
ideas.pitch: Apply the same two frozen rules to the US small-cap index during the US session. One leg would carry both the market's intraday momentum and the intraday rotation between styles, which my check shows also trends but cannot be traded as a two-leg spread.
ideas.mechanism: Same forced hedging as on us100 (leveraged small-cap ETFs, index options), plus rotation: institutional programmes that shift money between styles are worked through the day, so relative moves continue. In-sample, noise-area momentum on the us100/us30 ratio earns +2.29 bp gross per trade (t 3.15, positive 7 of 8 years); made beta-neutral it is still +1.7 to +1.9 bp (t 2.1-2.4). The payers are intraday pairs and mean-reversion traders. It persists because as a spread it costs 2.0-2.2 bp for two legs, more than it earns, so nobody at retail cost can take it; only a single volatile leg could. Counter-evidence: us500 with the same rule nets +1.1 bp (PF 1.09-1.125, t 1.6) and us30 nothing; picking the 'leading' US index each day nets +1.25 bp against +3.57 for us100 alone, so us100 is the special one.
ideas.role_of_ai: None in the decision; a plain algorithm. Same nightly statistical monitor as idea 1. No language-model call is needed.
ideas.instruments: US2000 (Russell 2000 CFD), US cash session only.
ideas.holding_time: 30 minutes to 6 hours, flat by 15:55 New York.
ideas.trades_per_day: About 1.3 a day, but only about 0.4 of an independent bet: in my replica us500 and us30 results correlate 0.50-0.65 with us100 on the same day. No visible change in the share of winning days.
ideas.edge_vs_cost: Trade standard deviation about 60 bp. Gross: 1.2 bp if us30-like, 3.2 bp if us500-like, 4.9 bp if us100-like. Cost: FP spread unknown; other brokers 0.3-0.5 point at an index near 2,500 = 1.2-2.0 bp, plus 0.4 slippage = 1.6-2.4 bp. Central net about +1 bp, PF about 1.08, which fails the PF 1.12 bar; a pass needs strength close to us100's.
ideas.first_experiment: Step 0: read spread and minimum lot in MT5. Step 1 (1 day on top of idea 1's pipeline, no API cost): Dukascopy USSC2000.IDX/USD one-minute bid/ask up to 2021 (check that at least 5 in-sample years exist), noise30 and ocm4 unchanged, 2 configurations logged, about 200 and 120 trades a year. Pass rule fixed now: the same lab criteria as idea 1, plus a spanning test: regress the sleeve's daily result on the two us100 sleeves' daily results and require the intercept to have t >= 2. Then one validation run.
ideas.kill_rule: Round trip above 2.2 bp; any in-sample criterion fails; spanning intercept t below 2 (then it is the us100 sleeves again at a higher cost).
ideas.differs_from_failed: Not the index-to-index lead-lag (failed) and not the two-leg style spread (I tested it: dead on cost). It is the frozen us100 rule on an index with a different driver mix; us500 and us30 failed with the same rule, which is the main reason the odds are low.

reviews.fatal_flaw: The proposal as written fails; only half of it is worth a test. (1) The sample is half what the designer assumed: Dukascopy JPN.IDX has no 09:00-10:00 Tokyo bars for most of 2015 and all of 2016-2017 (the feed starts at 10:00 JST), so only 2014 and 2018-2021 are usable: about 785 noise-area and 577 opening-candle trades, not 1,550 and 950. The stated power ('us100-like strength gives t 3.2') is wrong: with 785 trades even us100-like strength gives a gross t of about 2.2. (2) The noise-area leg is dead on cost: my replica gives +2.9 bp gross per trade (t 1.9 in bp, 2.4 in R), against a 1.6-3.6 bp round trip. Net is +1.3 bp (t 0.8-1.2, PF 1.09-1.13) at 1.6 bp and zero at 2.5 bp; the 10 best days carry 82 % of the gross total. (3) The opening-candle leg is strong in-sample but its last two years are flat: gross +13.1 / +15.8 / +8.0 bp in 2014 / 2018 / 2019, then +2.5 and +0.8 bp in 2020 and 2021 (without the stop: -0.5 and -9.8 bp). That is at or below cost for 250 consecutive trades just before the validation period. (4) The mechanism does not match the effect: leveraged-ETF rebalancing is a closing flow, yet 12:30-14:55 continuation after a big opening candle is -0.4 bp. From memory, not re-verified: the Bank of Japan bought ETFs after weak mornings through most of 2014-2021 and stopped in 2024, and the Tokyo close moved from 15:00 to 15:30 in November 2024, so the frozen 15:00 clock is wrong for the last validation year and for live trading. (5) What survives adds about 0.4 trade a day (96 a year), not 1.3, and no extra winning days. A demo verdict would take about 3 years (about 290 trades for t = 2 at 0.15 R per trade).
reviews.strongest_point: The opening-candle rule transferred with nothing tuned and shows a real-looking in-sample effect: +7.6 bp gross per trade and +0.197 R (t 3.7 in R, 2.7 in bp) on 577 trades. Both sides are positive (long +7.3, short +7.9 bp). The 3- and 5-minute neighbours agree (+9.8 and +7.0 bp). Filled one minute late it keeps +6.4 bp, so it is not a first-tick artefact, and one-minute autocorrelation at the open is about zero (no stale-index catch-up). In R terms it clears t >= 2.5 up to a 2.5 bp cost (t 3.1 at 1.6 bp, 2.7 at 2.5 bp). Independence is confirmed: daily correlation with the us100 sleeves is +0.10 same date and 0.00 against the previous US session. ideas.name: Tokyo-fix dealer: sell USD/JPY at the 09:55 Tokyo fixing, cover two hours later
ideas.pitch: Every Tokyo morning, banks buy dollars for customers whose orders are priced at the 09:55 fixing, which pushes USD/JPY up into 09:55; once the flow is done the price falls back over about two hours. The robot sells USD/JPY at 09:55 Tokyo time and covers at 11:55, either every weekday (A) or only on the heavy settlement days called gotobi (B: the 5th, 10th, 15th, 20th, 25th and month-end).
ideas.mechanism: WHO PAYS: Japanese importers, investment trusts and other bank customers whose dollar purchases are executed at the 09:55 fixing whatever the price; settlement custom concentrates them on gotobi days. Banks pre-buy, the price peaks at the fix, then reverts. WHY IT PERSISTS: the flow is a business convention, not a view. Krohn, Mueller and Whelan (Journal of Finance 2024, 1999-2019, nine currencies) document a dollar run-up before each fixing and a fall after it, and read the reversal as dealers' pay for carrying inventory risk. WHY FASTER PLAYERS DO NOT TAKE IT ALL: it is not a speed trade. The reversal takes two hours, earns about 2 bp against 16-18 bp of risk per trade, and in that paper disappears at full quoted spreads (Sharpe 0.1 to 1.0 at half spreads). The user's all-in cost of about 0.9 bp is far below those spreads. AGAINST: the same paper finds the Tokyo reversal smaller after 2014, and the gotobi trade is now widely described on broker sites.
ideas.role_of_ai: None in the trading decision, and I will not pretend otherwise. Plain algorithm: clock rule, gotobi and Japanese-holiday calendar, disaster stop, cost guard, kill rule, nightly re-estimate of run-up and reversal for monitoring only. Language model: (1) once a year drafts the gotobi, bank-holiday and Bank of Japan meeting calendar, which code then checks; (2) writes the evening phone report; (3) optional forward-only experiment after go-live: before 09:50 Tokyo it reads public headlines for intervention warnings or a Bank of Japan surprise and marks 'stand aside'. That skip is logged but not obeyed until at least 60 skipped days show the skipped days are worse than the taken ones. About one call a day, under 1 USD a month.
ideas.instruments: USDJPY on the FP Markets Raw account in MT5; the 0.01-lot minimum is 1,000 USD notional, so any account size works. Venue note: Interactive Brokers spot FX would roughly halve the cost (about 0.45-0.55 bp) but only for tickets of 100,000 USD or more, because of its 2 USD minimum commission; that needs an account of roughly 20,000 USD or more and a robot outside MT5. Not needed for the test.
ideas.trades_per_day: A: 1 per weekday. B: about 0.28 (6 a month). It adds to the existing 4-5 trades a day; it does not replace them.
ideas.holding_time: 2 hours (00:55 to 02:55 UTC, no daylight-saving shift in Tokyo); always flat by 11:55 Tokyo time.
ideas.data_needed: Dukascopy USDJPY one-minute bid/ask, already in the lab (/home/user/gold-orb/lab/data/fp/usdjpy_m1.parquet, 2013 onward). Public Japanese bank-holiday calendar and Bank of Japan meeting dates. For the live check, FP's own spread around 09:55 Tokyo (02:55 or 03:55 server time).
ideas.edge_vs_cost: In-sample 2013-2021, lab frame with FP costs, my run today. A: 2,340 trades, gross +2.11 bp (t 5.7), cost about 0.92 bp (spread plus commission 0.71 median, plus 0.2 slippage), net +1.19 bp (t 3.2), win rate 52 %, 56 % of months positive, worst trade -81 bp, worst drawdown -382 bp. Yearly net totals in bp: +661, -5, -18, +751, +610, +175, +53, +635, -79, so four strong years and five flat. B: 648 trades, gross +3.42, net +2.51 bp (t 2.9), win rate 57 %, 69 % of months positive, 8 of 9 years positive. One day, the Brexit vote on 24 June 2016, made +428 bp; without it A nets +1.01 (t 3.1) and B +1.86 (t 3.4). The turn is at the fixing minute: +0.80 bp in 09:30-09:55 (t 4.9), then -0.77 bp in 09:55-10:05 (t 6.1); 09:55 ranks first of 96 placebo start times between 07:00 and 15:00. reviews.fatal_flaw:
Not fatal, but configuration A (every weekday) is broken as stated and the edge is thinner than presented. Five points, all from in-sample data (2013-2021).

1. Only 40 % of the gross is fixing flow. On Japanese working days the sharp reversal 09:55-10:05 is +0.88 bp (t 6.6); it is +0.56 bp on ordinary days and +1.69 bp on gotobi days. That is below the round-trip cost on ordinary days: a 10-minute trade nets -0.09 bp at lab cost. The other +1.31 bp comes from a slow drift 10:05-11:55. That drift is just as large on 124 Japanese bank holidays (+2.18 bp), when there is no fixing. So it is the general Tokyo-hours yen drift, which the lab already rejected in coarse form (USDJPY -1.7 bp, below cost), not 'that effect diluted'.

2. The cost is probably understated by about 0.22 bp. The lab frame uses 1.1 pip all-in for USDJPY (0.71 bp). FP's 6 USD per lot commission is 0.6 bp of 100,000 USD, which is 0.93 pip at a price of 155, not 0.6 pip. With the 0.52 pip Raw spread that gives about 1.45 pip, or 0.94 bp, and 1.14 bp with slippage. This is my arithmetic from the published commission; it needs confirming in MT5.

3. At the corrected cost A is B plus a tail with no edge. A nets +1.01 bp (t 2.6), 5 of 9 years positive. The 1,379 trades that are neither gotobi nor Friday net +0.24 bp (t 0.5), 4 of 9 years. At the lead's 1.5 bp figure A nets +0.63 bp (t 1.6).

4. The net profit is a volatility-regime effect. With the trailing 20-day volatility of the same window above its running median (28 % of days) the net is +2.30 bp; on the other 72 % it is +0.16 bp (t 0.5). The five quiet years (2014, 2015, 2018, 2019, 2021) net +0.13 bp at lab cost. The top 23 days (1 %) make 2,116 of 2,787 bp in total; these are the Brexit vote, the 2016 US election and March 2020, i.e. yen safe-haven days, not fixing flow.

5. Competition and power. The gotobi trade is standard fare on Japanese retail FX sites, and those traders pay about 0.2 pip with no commission, roughly a seventh of this user's cost. The clean 10-minute reversal fell from about 1.1 bp (2013-2017) to about 0.7 bp (2018-2021). The designer's power figures of 65 % and 75 % are too high once the cost is corrected and the higher USDJPY volatility after 2021 is allowed for; I estimate 30-45 % even if the in-sample edge is fully intact. Live trading can never confirm it: at +1 bp against 17 bp of noise, t = 2 needs about 1,150 trades, 4.5 years for A and longer for B.

It also gives the user none of what he asked for: no AI, about 0.3 to 1 trade a day, 51-57 % winning trades, and a prize of roughly 1-3 % a year per 1x notional.
reviews.strongest_point: The gross effect is real and the mechanism checks out on a placebo the designer did not run. On 124 Japanese bank holidays the pre-fixing run-up (09:30-09:55) is -1.59 bp and the 10-minute reversal is -0.10 bp; on 2,152 working days they are +0.98 bp (t 5.7) and +0.88 bp (t 6.6). The fixing-specific part therefore follows the Japanese banking day, as the flow story requires, and it is two to three times larger on gotobi days (run-up +1.92 bp, reversal +1.69 bp). 09:55 ranks first of 288 five-minute start times across the whole day. With 1 % trimmed from both tails the 2-hour gross is still +1.78 bp (t 6.5). B is positive in 8 of 9 years at the corrected cost: +1.96 bp (t 2.3), or +1.30 bp (t 2.4) without the Brexit day. There is a peer-reviewed prior (Krohn, Mueller and Whelan, Journal of Finance 2024). No language model is in the decision, so the memory-leak warning does not apply. The data is already in the lab, the rule is a clock rule with no look-ahead, the pass rule is fixed in advance, and the answer is known in one or two days at zero cost. The designer was honest about fragility, the 110 cells looked at, and the absence of any AI role.
reviews.better_variant:
Drop A as a tradeable configuration and still spend the one day on the validation run, with these changes.

1. Before any validation run, correct the USDJPY cost in the frame to about 1.45 pip all-in, and read FP's actual spread at 00:55 UTC and the commission per lot in MT5.
2. Pre-register B (gotobi, shifted back over weekends and Japanese holidays) as the primary configuration. If a second shot is wanted, use 'gotobi or Friday' instead of A: in-sample 804 trades, +2.33 bp net at corrected cost, t 3.3, 9 of 9 years. ideas.name: Sleeve factory with a false-discovery budget (AI researches and engineers; frozen rules trade)
ideas.pitch: Use the AI the way Man Group and Two Sigma say they do: it proposes hypotheses with a stated payer, codes them, attacks them and maintains the MT5 robot, while every order comes from a frozen rule that passed a pre-registered gate. The robot learns at the timescale the statistics allow: sleeves are added, put on probation on demo, funded and retired on written evidence rules, quarter by quarter.
ideas.mechanism: The money comes from the mechanisms the existing sleeves already exploit: intraday trend created by hedging and forced flows on the Nasdaq, and breakout continuation on retail-heavy, high-volatility markets (bitcoin, ether, gold). The payers are hedgers and late chasers, not a counterparty the AI outsmarts. Faster players leave it because each sleeve is small, noisy (about 45 % winning trades, profit concentrated in a few trend days) and held for hours. What the AI adds is throughput and discipline: about 1,500 configurations tested with every trial logged. The process is the only thing in the lab with out-of-sample support. From the stored round-2 verdicts, 9 of 14 validated sleeves passed, but they are only about 3 independent effects out of 6 clusters. A rough pooled z across the six clusters is about 1.9 (my calculation; round-1 gold sleeves are not in that file). That is suggestive, not proof.
ideas.role_of_ai: The AI (offline, no latency constraint): reads literature and data documentation; writes each hypothesis with a "who pays" paragraph and one frozen configuration; codes it to the lab's make_orders contract; runs the in-sample gate and null tests; runs an adversarial review (entry delayed, costs x1.5, every-signal); translates the rule to MQL5 plus a Python twin; writes the evening report. Plain algorithm: every entry, stop, exit and size in MT5 (0.1-0.3 s). Never the AI: picking or vetoing a trade, re-tuning after validation, looking at the holdout.
ideas.instruments: Existing sleeves: us100, gold, bitcoin, ether. Next batches, as frozen transfers of the two mechanisms that passed (never new tuning): oil, Asian indices, silver and other liquid crypto CFDs, only where the cost is at most a quarter of the in-sample gross edge.
ideas.trades_per_day: 4-5 today (22 a week in the 1,000 EUR replay). Possibly 5-7 if one or two sleeves are added within a year. No promise of more.
ideas.holding_time: us100 sleeves 2-4 hours; crypto 1-18 hours; gold trend sleeves up to two days. Mostly intraday, not strictly.
ideas.edge_vs_cost:
**In-sample net edge per trade (trade files, before 2022)**
- us100: +4.0 and +4.6 bp against a 0.8 bp cost.
- Gold: +4.3 to +10.8 bp against 1.1 bp.
- Bitcoin follows Nasdaq: +10.9 bp against 4 bp.
- On indices and gold, cost is not the risk; decay is.

**Crypto in validation**
- The 72-hour bitcoin breakout earns 3.4 bp gross against about 7 bp of cost. It is positive only in R terms.
- Ether earns 12.7 bp gross against 11-15 bp.
- The ridge-filtered breakout holds +0.13 / +0.09 R per trade.

**Portfolio in validation**
- About +0.07 R per trade over 4,638 trades. I derived this from the replay (1,000 to 18,175 EUR at 1 % risk); the period flatters it.
- After shrinkage for selection, a fair forward expectation is +0.03 to +0.05 R per trade, or roughly PF 1.05-1.15.
ideas.first_experiment:
**(a) The single 2026 holdout look, already planned**
- Frozen portfolio, pass if PF > 1, as written in the lab's protocol.
- A zero-edge portfolio passes this about half the time, so it can kill but not confirm.
- Expected z is only about 1: roughly 1,000 trades, about 600 independent, at +0.05 R with a standard deviation of 1.2 R.
- Half a day of work, no API cost.

**(b) Factory batch 1**
- 20 hypotheses, one frozen configuration each (at most 5 logged variants), written before any data is touched.
- In-sample gate unchanged; at most 4 validation shots.
- Survivors go to demo at quarter size for at least 150 trades or 3 months.
- Batch-level rule, fixed in advance: success means at least 2 validation passes from independent mechanisms. One pass is what chance gives (4 shots x about 24 % pass rate under zero edge).
- About 6-8 days of AI work, about 30-60 USD of API.
ideas.kill_rule:
- **Portfolio:** stop and return to demo if 2026 holdout PF < 1; or if forward mean R is at or below -0.03 after 600 trades (2 % false-kill risk if the true edge is +0.07 R); or if drawdown exceeds 1.5 times the validation maximum (33.9 % at 1 % risk).
- **Factory:** closed for an asset class after two consecutive batches (40 hypotheses) without a validation pass.
- **Sleeve:** retired if its measured live cost eats more than half of its validation net edge.
- No re-tuning on validation or holdout data, ever.
ideas.differs_from_failed: It proposes no new prediction rule and keeps the AI out of the trade decision, where all three blind tests failed. It formalises the only process that produced passes and adds what earlier rounds lacked: a per-batch chance baseline, a cap on validation shots, a forward demo stage and written retirement rules.

ideas.name: Operating layer that learns execution, not direction (nightly AI supervisor, live cost learning, paper shadow league)
ideas.pitch: What a robot can honestly learn day by day is its own costs and execution, because that is measured in basis points on every fill; an edge of +0.05 to +0.1 R takes hundreds of trades to see. The AI supervises the rule robot every night and reports to the phone, a plain rule adapts to live spreads, and any direction-picking AI (a learned scorecard, the language model) runs on paper beside the robot until a paired forward test promotes it.
ideas.mechanism:
There is no new counterparty. The loss being fought is implementation shortfall, which the user pays to the broker and to the clock.
- **Timing:** the lab's delay stress shows about 0.4-0.5 bp of the us100 band rule's 4 bp sits in the first minute after each check. On the 5-minute opening-candle variant, 1.8 of 6.5 bp sits in a single minute.
- **Crypto spreads:** the modelled crypto spreads are provisional. +2 bp puts the bitcoin breakout at the pass bar, +7.3 bp at break-even; ether breaks even at +15 bp.
- **Outside evidence:** the six-month fleet study (arXiv 2609.05663) found the operating layer, not the strategy text, drove outcomes; a mechanical bracket was worth +39 bp per position.

It persists because retail robots are rarely reconciled against their backtest. Nobody competes for it: it is the user's own leak.
ideas.role_of_ai:
**Language model (one call a night, under 10 USD a month)**
- Reads the day's fills and the twin backtest replayed on the broker's own bars.
- Explains every mismatch (missed signal, late fill, spread spike, clock change, contract specification change).
- Writes the evening phone report and proposes code fixes for review.
- Is tested monthly with a seeded fault.

**Plain algorithm**
- Keeps a running average of spread and slippage per sleeve at decision times.
- Skips an entry when the live spread exceeds twice the modelled one (threshold fixed in advance).
- Sizes by the frozen rule, never by recent profit.

**Paper only**
- A ridge scorecard (half or one-and-a-half size per signal) and a language-model verdict are logged on every live signal and never traded before promotion.
ideas.instruments: The instruments of the validated sleeves on the FP Markets account: us100, gold, bitcoin, ether.
ideas.trades_per_day: Adds none. It supervises the 4-5 a day of the rule portfolio, and the spread gate may skip a few per cent of them.
ideas.holding_time: Unchanged: 1 hour to 2 days, depending on the sleeve.
ideas.edge_vs_cost:
**No gross edge by design. The stake:**
- us100 and gold sleeves net 4-11 bp per trade, so each 0.5 bp of unmodelled slippage costs 5-12 % of their profit.
- The five crypto sleeves live or die on 2-15 bp of spread that has never been measured on the live feed.

**The overlays are small (in-sample checks I ran, before 2022 only)**
- Scorecard on the us100 and gold sleeves, walk-forward out of fold, 2,899 trades: top half +0.122 R, bottom half +0.070 R, positive in 4 of 6 years, z about 1.2. Not significant. Even if real, it is worth +0.013 R per trade (about +0.5 bp on us100).
- Re-weighting sleeves by recent profit: Sharpe 2.35 at equal weight against 1.98 (weights by trailing 3-month R) and 2.20 (on/off). After a losing trailing window the next month is still +1.0 to +1.1 R per sleeve. Caveat: the sleeves were selected on the full sample, which biases this against re-weighting.
ideas.first_experiment:
**Stage 1: four weeks on the FP demo** (about 90-100 trades, 3-4 days of work since the bridge, twin and journal comparison exist, under 10 USD of API)
- Run the frozen sleeves through the existing MT5 bridge and log bid / ask at every decision time.
- Pass rule, fixed in advance:
  - at least 90 % of twin entries matched within one minute;
  - mean slippage against the twin at most +0.5 bp on us100 and gold, +2 bp on bitcoin, +7 bp on ether;
  - no unexplained position;
  - the supervisor catches one seeded fault.

**Stage 2: four weeks live at minimum lot**
- Same thresholds. Demo fills are optimistic, so this stage is the one that counts.

**Shadow league**
- Paired statistic: mean of (weight - 1) x R over signals.
- Read once at 1,000 signals (about 11 months). Promote only if z >= 2.5 and the effect is positive in at least two of three instrument groups.
- Honest power: for the scorecard's in-sample-sized effect the expected z is only 0.7-1.6. Most likely outcome: not promoted.
ideas.kill_rule:
- **Sleeve:** retired, not re-tuned, if after 100 demo and 100 minimum-lot trades its measured cost exceeds the model by more than half of its validation net edge.
- **Spread gate:** removed if the trades it skips turn out to earn at least the average (checked at 200 skips).
- **Supervisor:** replaced by a fixed template if it misses a seeded fault or raises more than one false alarm a week.
- **Shadow arms:** stopped for futility at 1,000 signals if z < 1. Never promoted on fewer than 1,000 paired signals.
- **Size:** nothing changes position size because of recent profit or loss.
ideas.differs_from_failed: Every failed attempt tried to learn direction: boosted trees on 1-20 minutes, the language model as judge, chart reader and news reader, reshaped exits. This learns costs, where the noise is basis points and 20-50 fills give an answer. Direction overlays are confined to paper, with a paired test on identical signals that uses only data after the model's cut-off, so the leak problem does not arise.

dropped_by_designer: Language model as discretionary trader (Alpha Arena style, with or without news): four of six models lost 42-59 % in 17 days, the winner changed between seasons, a six-month fleet won 41 % of round trips against 50 % for retail, and the lab's three blind tests were negative. About 4 %; kept only as a paper shadow arm.

Language model scoring share headlines for next-day drift (Lopez-Lira and Tang): the best-supported reading result, but concentrated in small caps and bad news, declining with adoption by the authors' own account, and it needs share CFDs (minimum commission; megacap opening rule -8 bp after costs). Only about four months of clean post-cut-off data. About 5 %.

Language model reading earnings releases (free SEC filings) for an open-to-close trade on earnings day: large moves relative to cost, but seasonal rather than daily, the same share-CFD cost problem, and the gap direction is a plain rule that needs no model. About 5 %.

Language model classifying central-bank text as hawkish or dovish: fewer than 20 independent events a year, the lab's macro-release rules failed validation, and its own post test showed the move is over before post + 2 minutes.

Re-weighting sleeves day by day on recent profit ("learns which rule is working"): my in-sample check gives Sharpe 2.35 at equal weight against 1.98 and 2.20 for the adaptive versions. Detecting a dead +0.1 R sleeve takes about 250-660 trades, so daily learning about edge is statistically impossible.

Ridge scorecard filter on the us100 and gold sleeves as a stand-alone idea: in-sample out-of-fold gain +0.05 R between halves, z about 1.2, per-sleeve p-values 0.09, 0.76, 0.32, 0.02 and 0.64. It would not earn a validation shot as it stands; the lab's ML track already found the filter works on crypto only. About 10 %; kept as a paper shadow arm.

Reinforcement learning, deep nets or time-series foundation models predicting short-horizon returns: the same target as the lab's failed 1-20 minute study (51-56 % right against 55-75 % needed). I found no live after-cost evidence, and FINSABER shows simple rules beat the learned strategies on long samples.

Copying published agent frameworks or contest-winning prompts (multi-agent "hedge fund" repositories, the Qwen or Grok setups): their backtests are contaminated by memory (Look-Ahead-Bench, KTD-Fin) and the contest wins are 14-17 day samples.

Letting an agent mine thousands of factors without a trial budget (RD-Agent style): the evidence is backtest only, and Two Sigma names multiplying hypotheses as the main risk. Kept only inside the factory with a capped number of trials and validation shots.
Language-model forecasting on prediction markets: models are improving there, but these are not MT5 instruments and not what the user asked for.
Limit orders in place of market orders on time exits to save the spread: if price is a martingale, "limit, else market after a timeout" has zero expected gain and only adds variance.

reviews.name: Sleeve factory with a false-discovery budget (AI researches and engineers; frozen rules trade)
reviews.fatal_flaw:
Not fatal, but the proposal splits into a core that holds and an expansion that is largely pre-refuted.

1. The 'next batch' has mostly been tested already and failed. Stored results: the gold 4-hour Donchian rule transferred to oil passed in-sample (PF 1.34, t 2.47) and then scored PF 0.60, t -3.19, 0 of 4 years in validation; silver has a gross edge but costs leave nothing (net PF 0.73-0.98); the us100 intraday rules do not survive on us500 or us30; four frozen transfers on eight currency pairs give basket PF 0.92-0.98; the opening rules fail on the 40-share basket. The last eight tracks (fx, stocks, dip, shape, vol, overnight, idx_eu, pivots/Bollinger: about 580 logged configurations) produced zero validated sleeves. The factory's marginal yield is close to zero, and its three passing clusters are all published effects.

2. The batch success rule does not control false discoveries. With 4 validation shots and a 17-24 % chance pass rate each, 'at least 2 passes' happens 14-25 % of the time with no edge at all. Every new batch also re-uses the same 2022-2025 window, which already has dozens of logged accesses, so validation is slowly becoming in-sample.

3. The 2026 holdout is not a clean single look. It was already opened on 2026-11-05 for the two gold sleeves (43 and 70 trades, PF 1.53 and 1.25, t 1.05 and 0.59), and 2026 gold and us100 data were used in the language-model tests. As the designer admits, PF > 1 passes about half the time under zero edge.

4. Truth arrives slowly. Separating +0.04 R per trade from zero at 2 sigma needs about 3,600 trades (sd 1.2 R), roughly 3 years at 22 trades a week, longer with correlated sleeves (I measured 0.49 same-day correlation between the two us100 sleeves and 0.46 between bitcoin and ether breakouts in-sample). The forward kill rule (mean R at or below -0.03 after 600 trades) lets a zero-edge portfolio continue 73 % of the time. The drawdown kill sits at about 51 % of the account.

5. Fit with the brief is poor on three points. The payoff is the opposite of 'many tiny gains': in-sample the top 5 % of trades make 206 % (noise bands) and 169 % (opening candle) of the us100 net profit, and only 41-42 % of trade days win. The 1,000 EUR replay was under water for its first 14 months (trough -33.5 %) and 2024 alone multiplied the account by 4.6. Minimum lots (about 12 USD risk per us100 or bitcoin trade, 35-55 USD on the gold Donchian) mean the account size is not irrelevant: 538 trades were skipped for minimum lot in that replay.
reviews.strongest_point: It is the only item with out-of-sample support, and it keeps the language model out of the trade decision where three blind tests failed. Cost is not the binding constraint on the core sleeves (us100 +3.9 and +4.4 bp net in-sample against 0.8 bp; I recomputed these from the trade files). The designer's own numbers check out: 9 of 14 sleeves and 3 of 6 clusters passed validation, pooled cluster z about 1.9, and the chance of 3 or more of 6 clusters passing under zero edge is about 10 %. The us100 mechanism is documented (Zarattini, Aziz and Barbon 2024; Baltussen et al. on hedging demand) and the two sleeves' validation t-values (1.89 and 2.32) are the best evidence in the lab.
reviews.better_variant:
Keep the core, cut the expansion.
- Trade only the clusters whose validation survives cost stress: us100 (two sleeves, counted as one bet), gold trend, and the ridge-filtered crypto breakout only once live spreads are measured. Drop the plain 72-hour bitcoin breakout now (net -4 bp per trade in validation by the lab's own figures).
- Stop spending the 2022-2025 window. Any new sleeve is judged on forward data only (demo or minimum lot), with a lifetime alpha budget: for example t at or above 2 on at least 250 forward trades, and the number of candidates ever admitted written down.
- Replace 'at least 2 passes of 4' with a rule whose false-positive rate is stated and below 5 %.
- Tell the user plainly that the forward verdict takes 1 year if the edge is +0.07 R and 3 or more years if it is +0.04 R, and size risk at 0.25-0.5 % until then.
- Use the factory time for transfers not yet refuted only, and write the refuted list (oil, silver, us500, us30, DAX, FX, shares) into the protocol.

reviews.name: Operating layer that learns execution, not direction (nightly AI supervisor, live cost learning, paper shadow league)
reviews.fatal_flaw:
It contains no edge and can only subtract, and several of its tests are weaker than they look. It survives as a necessary module of the first idea, not as an idea on its own.

1. The slippage test is noise-dominated as written. 'Mean slippage against the twin at most +0.5 bp' on about 25-40 us100 entries in four weeks: the one-minute move at the us100 open has a median absolute size of 5 bp (lab file), so the standard error of that mean is about 0.4-0.8 bp, the same size as the threshold. The result would be a coin flip. Slippage must be measured against the requested price or the quote at send time, not against the twin's bar.

2. Demo fills prove nothing about costs, as the designer concedes, so stage 1 only tests the plumbing. Stage 2 at minimum lot is not small: about 12 USD risk per us100 or bitcoin trade and 35-55 USD on the gold Donchian.

3. The crypto-spread question does not need eight weeks. It needs no trades at all: the broker's own quotes can be logged from MT5, and the terminal's tick history (if FP Markets serves it for BTCUSD and ETHUSD, to be checked) answers it in an afternoon.

4. The spread gate cannot be evaluated by its own kill rule. If it skips 3 % of 4.5 trades a day, 200 skips take about four years, and a 200-trade mean has a standard error of about 0.085-0.1 R against an effect of about 0.05 R. It is also dangerous for trend sleeves: wide spreads coincide with the violent moments, and in-sample the top 5 % of trades carry 169-206 % of the us100 net profit.

5. The shadow league is an 11-month experiment with a foregone conclusion. The designer's own expected z is 0.7-1.6 against a bar of 2.5. The language-model arm repeats blind test 1 (6,174 signals, negative) on one sixth of the sample; the scorecard arm repeats a track where no model learned anything on us100 or gold (walk-forward PF 0.91-1.09).

6. The outside evidence is mis-transferred. arXiv 2609.05663 exists, but it studies language-model agents on memecoins and Hyperliquid perpetuals; the +39 bp bracket is a counterfactual on those agents' discretionary exits, and the paper's headline is that neither fleet shows a directional edge. It says nothing about reconciling a rule robot.

7. Effort is understated. The existing twin and expert advisor cover the gold Donchian only (/home/user/gold-orb/lab/live/ea_twin.py); ten more sleeves need twins, including a two-symbol trigger and a ridge scorecard. Expect 2-3 weeks, not 3-4 days. The robot also needs the Mac awake 24 hours a day, five days a week.
reviews.strongest_point: It attacks the most fragile assumption in the portfolio, with small noise. The lab's own files confirm the stakes: +2 bp of extra cost puts the 72-hour bitcoin breakout exactly at the PF 1.06 bar and +7.3 bp at break-even; ether breaks even at +15.2 bp; on the 5-minute opening-candle variant 1.82 bp of 11.8 bp sits in the first minute (I read 6.6 bp at two hours, matching the designer's 1.8 of 6.5). The paired forward design for any direction overlay is leak-free and correctly powered on paper, and the rule 'nothing changes size because of recent profit' is right. The designer's 10 % is honest about the absence of edge.
reviews.better_variant:
Reorder it so the cheap answers come first.
- Day 1: export the broker's tick or one-minute bid/ask history for bitcoin, ether, us100 and gold from the user's MT5 and recompute the crypto sleeves' in-sample cost sensitivity with the real spread at each decision time. Retire any sleeve whose cost eats more than half its net edge before a single order is sent.
- Test the spread gate in-sample on the existing frames (Dukascopy spread shape): are trades entered at more than twice the modelled spread worse than average? If not, drop the gate.
- Forward stage: go straight to minimum lot on the two cheapest instruments, measure slippage as fill minus requested price (stops) and fill minus quote at send (market orders); 30-50 fills per instrument then give a standard error near 0.1 bp.
- Keep the nightly supervisor as a deterministic reconciliation script; use the language model only to write the phone report and to draft fixes.
